history.heading: The first kings of a united Egypt
history.text:
The First Dynasty began with the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt under a king remembered as Menes, usually identified with Narmer. Much of what we know comes from objects carrying royal names, above all the Narmer Palette and the Narmer Macehead, whose scenes of victory over enemies have long been read as a record of the conquest of the Delta.

Power was centred on Thinis in Upper Egypt. The kings that followed included Hor-Aha, Djer, Djet and Den. Merneith, the mother of Den, received a tomb on the same scale as the kings' tombs close to those of Djet and Den, and may have ruled as regent, possibly as the first woman to govern Egypt.

history.heading: Tombs at Abydos and Saqqara
history.text:
The kings were buried in large tombs at Umm el-Qa'ab near Abydos, while great mudbrick tombs at Saqqara and Helwan, near Memphis, belonged to the elite of the new state. These early tombs were built mostly of wood and mud brick, with stone used only for some floors and walls.

A grim feature of the period was the burial of servants and animals around the royal tombs to serve the king in the afterlife: hundreds of subsidiary burials surround the tomb of Djer. The practice ended with the dynasty; the tomb of Qa'a, the last king, is the last with subsidiary burials.

history.heading: Early writing
history.text:
Hieroglyphic writing was still young and was used mainly for names, labels and short notes on objects such as year labels. Detailed records of the first two dynasties do not survive; the main later source is the terse annals of the Palermo Stone.

Modern radiocarbon studies place the reigns of Hor-Aha and Den around 3100–2900 BCE, consistent with the conventional dates used on this site.

history.heading: An obscure century
history.text:
The Second Dynasty is one of the least known periods of Egyptian history. Archaeological evidence is scarce, but comparing the First and Third Dynasties shows that this was a time of important institutional and economic development, laying the foundations of the centralised state of the Old Kingdom.

The early kings, Hotepsekhemwy, Raneb (Nebra) and Nynetjer, were probably buried in large underground gallery tombs at Saqqara, near the new administrative centre at Memphis.

history.heading: Horus and Seth
history.text: After Nynetjer the picture becomes confused. Some scholars think the country was divided and ruled by two lines of kings for a time. The king Peribsen broke with tradition by writing his name under the god Seth rather than Horus, the falcon god normally linked to the king, and he chose to be buried at Abydos, in Tomb P at Umm el-Qa'ab.

history.heading: Khasekhemwy reunites the land
history.text:
The last king, Khasekhemwy, wrote his name under both Horus and Seth, a sign that the two traditions had been reconciled. A statue base from Hierakonpolis shows slain enemies, recording a campaign against northern rebels.

Khasekhemwy was buried in Tomb V at Umm el-Qa'ab, and at Abydos he built a colossal mudbrick funerary enclosure, the Shunet ez-Zebib, which still stands. His successors of the Third Dynasty would translate such enclosures into stone.

history.heading: Building for eternity in stone
history.text:
The Third Dynasty opened the Old Kingdom, with its capital at Memphis. Its most famous king, Djoser, known in his own time by his Horus name Netjerikhet, made a revolutionary choice: to build his tomb not in mud brick but in stone.

At Saqqara his architect Imhotep stacked six mastaba-like stages into the Step Pyramid, about 62 m high, inside a vast walled complex whose stone buildings imitate structures of wood, reed and brick. Later generations honoured Imhotep as a sage, and by the Late Period he was worshipped as a god of healing.

history.heading: Djoser's successors
history.text:
Djoser's successor Sekhemkhet began a step pyramid of his own at Saqqara that was never finished. The so-called Layer Pyramid at Zawyet el-Aryan is usually attributed to Khaba. The last king of the dynasty was Huni.

These unfinished monuments show that the Step Pyramid was not a one-off: the kings of the Third Dynasty were developing the techniques of large-scale stone building that their successors of the Fourth Dynasty would take to the true pyramid.

history.heading: Kings and the sun god
history.text:
The kings of the Fifth Dynasty placed the sun god Ra at the heart of kingship. Beside their pyramids at Abusir, south of Giza, several of them built sun temples dedicated to Ra, beginning with the dynasty's founder, Userkaf.

Their pyramids were smaller than those of the Fourth Dynasty, but their temples were richly decorated with reliefs. Papyri found at Abusir, from the temple of Neferirkare, are among the oldest administrative archives to survive from Egypt and show in detail how a royal cult was run day to day.

history.heading: Expeditions and officials
history.text: Under Sahure, Egypt sent ships to the distant land of Punt for incense and other exotic goods, an expedition recorded in later annals. The administration grew, and officials outside the royal family took on more of the work of government; their large decorated tombs at Saqqara and Giza show scenes of daily life, farming and crafts in rich detail.

history.heading: Unas and the Pyramid Texts
history.text:
The last king, Unas, built a small pyramid at Saqqara whose burial chamber walls were, for the first time, covered with religious spells: the Pyramid Texts, the oldest body of religious writing from Egypt. They describe the king's journey to join the gods in the sky and were copied in the pyramids of later kings and queens.

After Unas the throne passed to Teti, the first king of the Sixth Dynasty.

history.heading: A new royal house
history.text:
Teti, the first king of the Sixth Dynasty, followed Unas on the throne. The later historian Manetho claims that Teti was murdered by his bodyguard; contemporary sources do not confirm it, but the story may explain the short reign of an ephemeral king, Userkare, attested between Teti and Pepi I.

Pepi I survived a conspiracy hatched in the royal harem, known from later records. His reign saw expeditions to Sinai, the alabaster quarries of Hatnub, the Wadi Hammamat, Punt and the cities of Byblos and Ebla in the Levant. He was followed by Merenre.

history.heading: Pepi II and Harkhuf
history.text: Pepi II became king as a boy and ruled for more than six decades; Manetho credits him with 94 years, one of the longest reigns in history. One of the most human documents of the Old Kingdom comes from his childhood: a letter he wrote to the expedition leader Harkhuf, copied on the wall of Harkhuf's tomb at Aswan, telling him to take great care of a dancing pygmy he was bringing back from the land of Yam.

history.heading: The end of the Old Kingdom
history.text:
Throughout the dynasty, the inscriptions in officials' tombs show the growing power of the nobility and of provincial governors, the nomarchs, who passed their offices on within their families. Royal authority weakened as theirs grew.

After the death of Pepi II, his many short-lived successors could not hold the provinces together. Manetho places a ruler named Nitocris at the end of the dynasty, a name now thought to come from a misreading of a king's name. Decentralisation led into the First Intermediate Period.
